6.title: The movie is ahead of its time in terms of effects, sound but not all of them are great.
6.content: It's not a genre I like, but I've heard about it a lot so I decided to check it out. And when I stepped into the movie, I felt like I was in a real, real place. Overall, what I found was great cinematography and effects, great sound, and great music. But the story of the movie I couldn't connect with it, really I had to try to be able to watch the whole movie. In particular, the part that I don't like the most in the movie is the flight scene and the communication between the pilots, not understanding what is going on, the hasty cutscenes, the lines keep on passing and the story ends.

6.title: See what an 80s pop movie looked like without the quirks
6.content:
Top Gun is a 80s classic.

The good. Interesting academy rivalry. Nice choice of music and score. Great footage of fighter planes. Beautiful San Diego photography. Funny scenes.

The actors. Tom Cruise plays the hothead excellently. Val Kilmer as his ice cool competitor is just perfect. However, the best and smoothest work is done by Meg Ryan. On the other hand, Kelly McGillis is unfortunately performed poorly and wasn't given much to work with. The rest of the cast does a pretty solid job. I'll just mention the better ones: Anthony Edwards, Tom Skerritt, and Michael Ironside. We can also see a small cameo by Tim Robbins.

The bad. Easy dialogs. Poor romance plot with lots of cliché and a weak female lead. A few continuity problems. Cockpit filming, lighting conditions mainly, doesn't correspond to fighter plane footage.

The ugly. Very awkward stick handling that looks ridiculous.

The result. A classic, mainly for those interested in seeing what really launched Cruise's career.

6.title: A necessary watch for the reboot, but not a necessary watch by itself
6.content:
I watched the original Top Gun the day before I went to go see the reboot. Overall, while it was a short movie, I understood the low rating despite it being a huge commercial success.

Thoughts

Haven't watched a lot of older movies but this movie felt very corny. Feel like half the movie is just close up of Tom. The romance build up was mediocre and I found the main theme playing every time they make contact was more hilarious. It is a good song, though.


Lots of jargons and aerial scenes that was a little hard to follow (The reboot fixes these problems very well). I can see how revolutionary this must have felt in the 80s. Most of the aerial scenes, however, felt like they were well done while feeling a little outdated. Final scene did make up for it. Very well done.


Over saturation.


Central plot and conflict is very weak. Zero tension on the progress of this "competition" for top gun. Part of that comes from the short running time. If the movie wanted to make sense, it should have been a little longer, and Goose's death come a little sooner. Character development was very weak for non adolescent viewers.


After watching the reboot, I feel like watching the original definitely helped me better appreciate the reboot. I'd almost call it a requirement to understand the central plot in the reboot. While this movie was a commercial hit, I am predicting that the new generation will appreciate the reboot more both commercially and critically.

6.title: Terrible love story, average drama, excellent action
6.content:
6/10 is the minimum score I deem a film to be 'worth watching'. Top Gun 1 i only watched as a warm-up to Maverick, which looks to be a superior film (will soon find out).

The first one has a poor love story, so cheesy and not in a fun charming way. The rest of the non-action drama is standard hokey fare. What makes the movie worth your time is the jet action: visceral camera, bombastic sound, clever editing. I watched the 3D-Bluray, the added depth worked well in those scenes. Felt quite immersive.

The cast are fine, they do what they can with the script. Tho' there's not really a convincing chemistry between the two romantic leads. Plot-wise, it's unclear who the antagonists are supposed to be, and why.

So the only reason to watch Top Gun 1 is for the flight action, and as a presumably-necessary prelude to the celebrated sequel.

6.title: Not anything special
6.content:
Although rather overrated and quite childish- Top Gun manages to squeeze some charm out of its macho premise making it a forgettable but not entirely pointless action spectacle that has continued to grow overtime. I'm gonna be honest and say I truly don't understand the hype or appeal of this movie to so many people. Sure, maybe it's just a nostalgia thing, but to many it seems much more than that when there is really so little to remember about this one. To start off with the things I didn't enjoy, the script is wire thin- but honestly that was to be expected. Some of the dialogue is so incredibly cheesey and played out, and much of the conflict on screen seems uninspired- and very derivative of other action films of a similar nature. The cinematography is an orange sunburn tan the entire course which has its moments, but certainty doesn't make it stand out. The soundtrack is rather good, but its overuse of the same two songs over and over again can be played out. Not to mention the second half of this movie takes a sharp right turn itself toward dramatic territory which is both unexpected and kinda undeserved. So what if anything positive is there to say about this one? Well for one, the actors do try their best. Tom Cruise is a delightful lead, as well as love interest Kelly McGillis as Charlie. The film can be entertaining to watch at times, and there are even a few moments that had me smile and even laugh at times which was surprising to me to say the least. If you turn your brain off and just go along for the ride, it's not half bad. In the end, Top Gun is no masterpiece but it is pure popcorn fun at times. Despite its struggles it manages to cook a half baked story into an entertaining action film just enough to leave you more satisfied than not. It may not deserve its popularity and high praised status but there certainly is much worse out there to compare it to.

My Rating: 5.7/10.

6.title: Why is this so revered?
6.content: Tom Cruise has definitely gotten better with age. He is okay here, but still learning. The story is also okay, and the plane sequences still hold up pretty well. So why don't I love this movie like so many my age? I saw it as a kid, and rewatching it now, maybe I saw it for what it is. A love story, with a tiny bit of action. The music is iconic from this movie, but I didn't realize how much they play the same annoying music over and over in almost every scene. I rewatched this alone in anticipation of the sequel because my wife had no interest, and honestly, I'm not sure about the sequel either at this point, though at the least it should look very cool 30 years later. So why do people go crazy for this movie, and I don't? Maybe because I'm Canadian, and the military doesn't get me pumped up.

6.title: Top Gun: The OG
6.content:
Definite list of shame item here I'm glad to check off. Unfortunately I feel like this suffers a lot from the hype that's built up around it. I know people that LOVE this movie and we're outraged I hadn't seen it and now that I have I don't really see what the big deal is. Well, aside from the fact that Tom Cruise doesn't age the same way as us humans, but I already knew that.

Top Gun is absolutely an embodiment of its time. It's big, loud, popcorn fare that is both dumb and smart at the same time. I bet this was a blast to see in theaters. Thing is, it also feels like an adolescent fantasy run rampant and I couldn't stop rolling my eyes at times. He's a brash, reckless fighter pilot that goes by his own rules, goofs off and has a very weird relationship with his teacher.

That said, there's also some serious weight at times. This came out over 30 years ago and back then they weren't afraid to hit you and get a little dark. Despite all the signs that were there, I was not expecting this to get as heavy as it did and I applaud it for that. Also, that song is still incredible and gave me goosebumps when it kicked in.

All in all, this is a fun little chunk of nostalgia. I love that it wasn't afraid to get its hands dirty, I just wish it would've grown up a little along the way. I could see my stance on this improving down the line as the hype machine fades for me but it's still an enjoyable enough experience worth checking out.

6.title: The Danger Zone
6.content:
I'm a little late to the Top Gun party.

Although fun, Top Gun does have its problems. But it's entertaining, has a few heavy-hitting moments, and is ultimately worth the watch thanks to some thrilling, if at-times hard to follow aerial action.

The cast is great in this movie. Tom Cruise thrives as cocky young hotshot Maverick, and Val Kilmer is great as his opposite who plays by the rules and hates Maverick's reckless style. There's some solid stuff between the two on screen.

I haven't seen anything else by director Tony Scott, but what we have here is solid if a bit frantic. The in-air action is fast and thrilling, so we definitely get a sense of scale, but it's at times too chaotic to follow. The crash scene involving Maverick and Goose was well done, and a scene where Maverick is on his motorcycle observing the jets has a series of fantastic shots as well.

The plot is serviceable, if a little thin. Watching it this day in age does make the characters feel a little thin, but it works. Maverick is haunted by the ghost of his father and not knowing what happened to him, and his reckless attitude eventually gets called into question by his best friend/RIO Goose. The love interest with Kelly McGillis' Charlie is typical but it works. There's not a lot of surprises in the story outside Goose's death.

Speaking of Goose's death, I knew he died going in, and the moment when it happened still surprised me. It's an effective well-done scene. One of the highlights of the film. From his death onwards is easily the most intriguing part of the movie.

Top Gun is worth checking out for the cool aerial shots, the awesome soundtrack, and the last act of the movie. Good performances all around, some fun to be had, and at times thrilling jet action. It's not a masterpiece by any means thanks to the generic story and generalized characters, but it's not a bad way to kill a few hours.

6.title: It has got the spirit!
6.content:
"You don't have time to think up there. If you think, you're dead"

As someone who was born in the late 90s; I have always envied those people who were born just before me, especially in the 80s. To me, those were the best times period. From all the catchy music to some amazing movies, and revolutionary fashion to trendsetting games; this decade had it all! Seeing Top Gun today (that too for the first time in my life); the film seemed to have brought me right back to that unforgettable period, and in all truthfulness, I couldn't be more pleased.

Now this film isn't extraordinary or something but it had enough material and substance to fulfill your appetite for entertainment! It's got a great soundtrack, exhilarating dogfights, and on top of all an admirable act from Tom Cruise who played his part with enough competence!

I loved how his character (Lt. Pete Mitchell aka Maverick) transitions from this reckless, cocky individual to a calm and level-headed being. It was a journey worth partaking!

Speaking of its demerits, well, to be honest, the only major criticism that I have is about its screenplay which could have had more pace and had it been a bit more tight, we as viewers could have been on the edge of our seats for the whole runtime! Moreover, all the technical terms and phrases may as well overwhelm a certain section of the audience, as it could often get detailed and adamant with its terminologies!

You don't need to be an a specialist, but I feel, you got to have some basic understanding of the subject, or else you wouldn't be able to enjoy this 'Aerial Ride' to its fullest!

6.title: Good, yet flawed, fun movie.
6.content: Was "Top Gun" an exciting joyride or macho b.s.? Whether or not you'll like "Top Gun" will depend entirely on rather or not you can manage to shut off your brain long enough to stand: (a) an extremely predictable story, (b) a rather idiotic love story, and (c) lots of crappy Ken Loggins/mid-80's music. The extremely predictable story is actually the easiest of the three flaws to overlook. Why? Because we grow to like all the characters in the movie. Maverick (Tom Cruise) is cool. Goose (Anthony Edwards) is the best buddy we all wish we had. Viper (Tom Skerritt) is the tough, yet fair, instructor. We even like Ice Man (Val Kilmer) by the end of the movie (the character's disdain for Maverick isn't because Ice Man's a jerk, but because he's concerned that Maverick is too unsafe). The stupid love story is a little harder to swallow. Kelly McGillis couldn't act her way out of a paper bag. Supposedly she has a Ph.D. in astrophysics (!), but somehow I doubt it. There's NO chemistry between the two characters. They profess to be in love, but the way it's portrayed in the movie, you get they feeling it's just about physical attraction (but, then again, who can blame them). Oh, and yes, the music in this movie sucks. Even the main non-Loggins score. Horrible. So what was good about "Top Gun"? Well, besides the cool characters (except Charlie), this movie has a lot of exciting flight sequences. This movie's not boring. Very, very fun to watch. (Except all the scenes with Tom Cruise with his shirt off...but I guess they had to give the women of 1986 something to watch, too.) Overall, 7 out of 10.

6.title: Re-watching this film after 10 years has made me realise how flawed and ordinary it was.
6.content:
Top Gun (1986) : Brief Review -

Re-watching this film after 10 years has made me realise how flawed and ordinary it was. I was in college 10 years ago when I saw Top Gun for the first time. By that time, I hadn't seen thousands of classics, so I enjoyed watching it. I enjoyed the aerial action, the adventure stuff, Tom's handsome looks and Kelly's sexy appeal. I didn't know much about the art of filmmaking. I didn't know there were aerial action classics like the Oscar-winner "Wings" (1927) and good films like Grant's "Only Angles Got The Wings" (1939), master Billy Wilders's "The Spirit Of St. Louis" (1957), and a few more in the 40s and 50s. But today, when I am through with almost 5000+ films right from 1901 to 2022, and those films mentioned above, I can easily notice the flawed aspects in Top Gun. Re-watching this film today has made a big difference in my viewing experience, and it has also shown me how mature my taste has become in the past 10-11 years. Top Gun looks so ordinary when I think about it as an aerial action drama and compare it to those old classics from the 30s and 40s. Not just story-wise, but many other factors too. First the story - what mediocre writing it is. Not a single moment of thrill. It was so predictable and cliched. Having a good friend and then losing him, a past that isn't known, a jealous colleague, a girlfriend who's in the same profession, getting nervous and that guilt after losing someone, I mean, all these things were outdated in the 70s only. What a great mess that love story angle was. And then, they had that typical reconciliation too. Seriously? How terrible does Tom look in some scenes with those immature expressions? The only thing that worked for me was the action part. That entire action portion in the last 15 minutes still looked great, despite the fact that I was re-watching it. Overall, it's a watchable action flick for action lovers, but nothing extraordinary. The box office success doesn't bother me because I have found many box office hits mediocre.

RATING - 6/10*

By - #samthebestest.

6.title: Stylish But Overrated Military Drama
6.content:
Never understood what all the hype was about. I upped my rating to six stars to be generous, and for Tom Cruise. I don't think it's the best military action drama film out there, and I think the 80s had lots of way cooler movies (think Lethal Weapon (1987) and Beverly Hills Cop (1984)). It's entertaining enough, even if it is slightly boring towards the middle.

The performances are good, so that's a plus. Tom Cruise is charismatic, and attacks his role, and you can just see him desperately wanting to move on to the other more popular movies in his future, which he could obviously see. Val Kilmer is good, if a little weird, and Kelly McGillis is good as the love interest, though I thought she was way better in Witness (1985). Only just now realizing that Tim Robbins was in this. He's one of those actors you see in a movie and like, then forget he was in it, then like him in another movie, and then eventually you have that moment where you realize all the movies he's actually done.

Tony Scott's direction, while undeniably more restrained than in his future works, is very nice, and it has his usual cool, glossy look. Scott was still finding his style at the time, but this is definitely a Tony Scott film. He's all over it, and it's one of the movie's high points.

It's a bit of a stretch to call this an action movie. It's more of a military drama. There's a training scene with the fighter jets in the beginning, but the only real action scene is a dogfight in the skies near the end, which is pretty cool, though it doesn't have anything on (kidding).

I really don't have much else to say about this. It's one of Cruise's best performances arguably, though I still believe to be his all-time best. It's a very 80s movie, and if you want to see a classic that is maybe a little overhyped, then go ahead. It's worth seeing once, just to see what everyone's talking about.

The flight scenes were the best bit and the romance and soundtrack were OK, but the plot and characterisation didn't cut it as well as I hoped it would. It seems so weak and badly written in that respect, as I watch it, unable to really grasp the lead of the film as I do with a good one.

Perhaps it just has to be seen as a light movie that satisfies different interests and tastes rather than anything too deep and in that respect it has aged well as a classic action/love/war thriller. But like the grindhouse movies of the 70s which just sold what they knew the viewers wanted to see, there are limits to the artistry of the film.

6.title: A Little Insight
6.content: Wanted to write this review because I didn't see this topic addressed in other reviews. With the exception of Kelly McGillis, the cast worked well for me. The forced and brief love affair could have been handled differently and, oh please, why did we have to sacrifice a pilot? Here's the parallel I draw: Top Gun absolutely sent me back to my brief time (as an activated reservist) in the military. Until the call-up to active status, I never noticed the blatant parallels with my time on active duty. My impression of my time was that although we were not fighter pilots, as an officer living and working amongst mostly other officers, there was, back in the day, a competition afoot! This movie came before my activation, but once in place in my unit, I noticed VERY striking parallels with the officers (pilots) in this movie and my peers and one superior officer in my midst. My time to be a soldier was a brief, 4 years after this movie's premier so maybe it was truly a sign of the times. My observation of a "boys club" in play was just as noticed as a parallel as was the spirit of competition. In fact, I remember wondering if this competition amongst military units within my branch of service was just "how it rolls." If so, then Top Gun falls right in line with what I observed as an outsider and short-timer suddenly thrust into active duty. The males in my unit were over the top with their macho personae, only offset by their male bonding, in spades. I had entered a boys club as a female. In a sense, Top Gun was my primer to learn about things to come in my active duty time ahead (of this movie's time). Glaring similarities to the movie's male characters is what I observed, but without the planes. Just sheer self-adoration, one-upmanship and an end result that absolutely befitted from the fruits of all the collective professional characters amongst me. A defacto Top Gun setting in real life, every day of my military time.

6.title: Take My Breath Away
6.content:
One day in the 1980s, top producer Jerry Bruckheimer sat in his office in Hollywood, flipping through the "California" magazine. He was mainly interested in an article about the US Navy's flight instruction school at Miramar Air Station in San Diego. The so-called TOPGUN program had started 20 years earlier (during the Vietnam War) and was rumored to be the place where the world's best fighter pilots trained. Which gave Bruckheimer an idea. So, he contacted the magazine's editor-in-chief and acquired the movie rights to the piece.

But it would be a challenging picture to make. In order to get the footage right, it was necessary for the film crew to cooperate fully with the US Navy. For the same reason, Jerry Bruckheimer (and his director Tony Scott) also had to allow the military's censor complete script approval. No wonder then that the picture became so strongly pro-armed forces. Ultimately, the US Navy actually used "Top Gun" as a recruiting tool in their search for new fighter pilots.

Unfortunately, in the '80s when "Top Gun" was made, CGI was still in its infancy. Tony Scott therefore had no opportunity to use computers to animate the many aerial sequences. The director briefly considered using miniatures instead, but dropped the idea because he suspected that it wouldn't look realistic enough. Consequently, actual planes performed real stunts in all the flying scenes in the movie. Tragically, though, a veteran aerobatic pilot was killed because of that.

Despite rather lukewarm reviews, "Top Gun" became a gigantic, international triumph. It was number one at that year's box office, while the film's soundtrack topped Billboard's Hot 200 album chart for five consecutive weeks. And the success just went on. Before he made "Top Gun", actor Tom Cruise had "just" been a hot commodity among others in Tinseltown. The movie elevated him to the next level, starting a decade of high-profile blockbusters.

6.title: The birth and death of the cool
6.content:
Tony Scott's "Top Gun" is arguably the most American movie ever made, which by pop culture laws translates to also the coolest movie ever made. This is about Kenny Loggins' brand of rock'n'roll, fighter jets, leather jackets, motorcycles, sunglasses during the night, macho rivalries, bromances and, of course, passionate love. What a thing.

The movie stars Tom Cruise as Maverick, a hotshot US Navy fighter jet pilot who is equal parts skill and attitude. He is a single-and-ready-to-mingle twenty-something years old ambitious but reckless and authority-defying young man. His partner Goose (Anthony Edwards) is the polar opposite--already married, he has no interest in showing off, but his friendship with Maverick is way too powerful to let that get in the way.

The beginning of the movie finds us flying, as we see Maverick and Goose flipped upside-down about two meters above a Russian MiG with Maverick flipping the Russian pilot off just because he can. Obviously, this reckless behavior doesn't go well with the brass which sends them to the US Navy's elite fighter weapons school to master the art of aerial dogfighting and also to get it out of their system. In there, Maverick meets Iceman (Val Kilmer). With his stiff hair and constant chewing--just to make sure he is cool enough--he is an equally brilliant pilot but also composed and by-the-book. Quickly, the two settle into a rivalry because rivalries are cool and you have the ultimate recipe for a full-blown cliché. There is just one thing missing: the girl. Enter Charlie (Kelly McGillis), astrophysicist and civilian Top Gun instructor with whom Maverick flirts before eventually both falling in love with each other.

Now, when "Top Gun" is in the air, it is unmatched. Scott uses the freedom of the open sky to his advantage by moving around at violent speeds, unbound by physical walls and surrounding the planes. The editing is based on generating brief shots of the pilot in moments in which he is put under pressure before furiously returning outside the cockpit freewheeling around shootouts. It does a great job at simulating the nauseating and overwhelming feeling of being in a dogfight--something which few people have ever experienced for real.

Unfortunately, after it lands, "Top Gun" simply doesn't know what to do with itself. The relationship between Maverick and Goose is honest but bland, the rivalry between him and Iceman--while containing obvious polarizing ideas--it's lost to a few brief interactions in which Maverick parades around like a child. But the biggest issue lies in his relationship with Charlie. At first, their flirts are combative--he uses his words to reel her in, she uses them as defenses and eventual counterattacks. But even after they get past adolescent woes, and share personal feelings--Maverick tells her about his missing father who was also a fighter jet pilot--they don't give in to each other, and it's Maverick the one who takes a step back.

I assume director Tony Scott took this strange decision to show us the guy is not all about "scoring" despite the fact that he wears aviator sunglasses more than 50% of the time. He is trying to tell us that Maverick is all about real love but I am pretty sure that by that point everyone believed that anyway. And also, when they eventually make out, it looks more stylized than a synth-pop track playing Saturday night at your local disco. This is also a pretty predictable movie--which comes naturally when you've got clichés--as when Maverick is on the verge of giving up on flying after suffering a personal loss, it's Charlie the one that picks him up and dusts him off. To be fair, I don't mind the predictability as by the time the movie gets to this point, it was clear to me what it is all about. I also like the message: it was love that saved Maverick--that, to me, is the biggest take from "Top Gun".

This is a spectacle to behold--a movie which is all about style, visually evocative despite being emotionally flat; it is brooding, dramatic, self-pitying and self-centered. These things don't particularly make for a good film, but at least they do factor in to contribute to what can only be called the American cool--which happens to be the best one.

6.title: "Top Gun" doesn't have a creative script and old clichés, exploring action scenes involving fighter jets and romance. Unlike the powerful images, the film never takes off
6.content:
"Top Gun" seems to have just one purpose: to elevate then-candidate Hollywood star Tom Cruise to stardom and, consequently, gross millions at the box office. And the uncreative script, written by Jim Cash and Jack Epps Jr., explores several clichés without any shame to achieve its objective. We have the promising young heartthrob who, due to the trauma of his past related to his father's death, has no fear or sense, but who, on the other hand, is incredibly good at what he does. We also have the girl (in this case a more mature woman) who will obviously get involved with the good guy and the annoying antagonist, who seems to exist only to generate conflict with the protagonist without apparent justification, and who will obviously become friends with him in the predictable ending. Finally, we have the jovial and romantic songs from Harold Faltermeyer's beautiful soundtrack, which remain stuck in the viewer's memory, reminding them of the film whenever they hear them (and at the time the romantic "Take my breath away", by the group Berlin, was played extensively on the radio). Just to reinforce the argument, notice the numerous times in which Scott uses close-ups of Tom Cruise, often wearing sunglasses, alternating with American shots (from the waist up) of the shirtless star, clearly exploring the charisma (and muscles) of the young actor to attract the female audience, as is evident in the volleyball game scene, which is nothing more than pure exhibitionism by the young heartthrobs. Even Goose's tense and sad death does not escape the cliché of the death of a best friend that serves as a turning point in the protagonist's life, perfectly symbolized in the scene in which Maverick throws his partner's ashes into the sea. And not even the pilot training sounds convincing, never conveying the expected difficulty that a pilot should face to reach the level of excellence required in a profession like this.

But "Top Gun" also has its positive points, starting with the excellent sound work, noticeable especially in the sensational aerial sequences, perfectly capturing the noise of planes tearing through the sky. Good editing by Chris Lebenzon and Billy Weber collaborates in these exciting sequences, where director Tony Scott creates beautiful shots, also helped by Jeffrey L. Kimball's photography direction and visual effects. The director takes advantage of the beautiful visuals during the flights, taking advantage of the universe of beautiful images that the sky provides to film from interesting angles such as the front, wing and tail of the planes. In another moment, Scott gives a close-up of Cruise when he talks about his late father, highlighting the sadness on his face when thinking about his mysterious death. Tom Cruise, in fact, has a good performance, demonstrating the usual energy as the rebellious Maverick, despite using endless smiles (obviously, trying to establish himself as a heartthrob). Notice how he smiles slightly when he hears that he is going to the special "Top Gun" school, as he knew that this was the opportunity of a lifetime to prove his quality as a pilot, in addition to being able to face his traumatic past. His performance grows in the final part, after losing his friend and leaving to overcome the trauma of the enigmatic loss of his father. But unfortunately, the predictable script doesn't demand much from the cast.

Goose, played by Anthony Edwards, has the sole function of causing forced laughter in the viewer and most of his weak dialogues with Maverick are not exciting, such as when they talk about the inverted Mig. Val Kilmer is caricatured and exaggerated as the one-dimensional Tom Kazanski, the "Iceman", who only has two human moments throughout the entire narrative. The first is when he respects Maverick's pain for losing his friend ("I feel for Goose") and the second is the predictable ending, when he finally recognizes the quality of his rival. Kelly McGillis plays the mature Charlotte and has her good moments, like when she tells Cruise that she didn't want to let their relationship get in the way of her profession ("I don't want you to know that I fell in love with you"). Her Charlotte, despite being completely in love, is very aware that assuming that passion could compromise her performance as a team instructor. Tom Skerritt is excellent as the intelligent commander Mike "Viper" Metcalf, who knows very well where Maverick can go and fights to get the best out of the boy. And finally, Meg Ryan steals the show in the few minutes she appears, playing Goose's wife, Carole Bradshaw. Totally loose and laid-back, she is clearly the best performance in the film, still conveying a lot of emotion when she loses her husband. It is with her on the scene that Goose and Maverick experience one of their best moments, when they sing together at the piano.

When Maverick approaches Charlotte and sings, helped by everyone in the bar, the song "You've lost that loving feeling", Tony Scott's film seems to excite. The excitement increases in the wonderful sequences starring fighter jets that cut through the sky at high speed. But unfortunately, when the action takes place on the ground, it is not successful, limiting itself to a common and uninteresting narrative. There's no problem using clichés, after all, they didn't become clichés for nothing. The problem is the way these are used, and unfortunately in this case the uncreative result is not pleasing, being saved only by the aforementioned aerial sequences. With exciting and impactful aerial sequences, "Top Gun" shows the danger and excitement that await each of the pilots at the Navy's prestigious fighter aviation school. Rewatching the film decades after its release still gives you that incredible, thrilling sensation with the wonderful aerial action scenes. Even though, nowadays, these scenes are not perfect, we must recognize the impact of the time of their release, however, the aerial scenes often seem confusing, filmed from a distance where we notice the use of models and other effects, especially in the destruction of the aircraft. The editing, in most of the aerial scenes, fails to create a visual game in which it shows the viewer who the character is under the pilot's outfit and the entire construction of the events that culminate in Maverick's impulsive and courageous actions, in the death of a character. Or in conflicts between pilots in full training. When we see it, the scene concludes and we accept what we only heard over the pilots' communications radio and from the Navy control cabin.

Interestingly, even before cinema took over the language of video games, "Top Gun" uses strategies to momentarily transform the viewer into an excited pilot shooting at enemy aircraft. Some of the moments with the greatest tension and sense of adventure are precisely in the aiming process that places our gaze directly on chasing the "villains" until everything is ready to detonate them with missiles. Tony Scott uses certain dramatic situations as mere subterfuges to accentuate an exciting vision of military equipment. In this sense, there is even an exaggeration in how Maverick is falsely trapped in a structure to rebel against. The instructors who reprimand him have deep admiration for him; the wife of a partner who dies on a mission is more concerned with consoling him than paying attention to her own pain; Maverick's questions about his beloved woman's opinions result in one thing: he's right. Even Iceman, the only one who seems realistic about his recklessness, is led to give in to his rival's exceptionalism. Therefore, the film exists to glorify Tom Cruise's character, to the point that his romantic advances are not considered. You don't have to go far to understand how problematic the invasion of the bathroom and the insistence on transforming a "no" into a "yes" are.

There are exciting situations in the production and nostalgia during the revisit can be responsible for relativizing certain problems in favor of a less demanding experience. However, if we look a little more carefully, we can see that not even the romance between Tom Cruise and Kelly McGillis' characters makes much sense. She is an officer openly flirting with a cadet and no one says anything, that is, breaking the rules is not even seen as a transgression; she is a figure that exists only to confirm how incredible he is, both in terms of his knowledge of flight and the intricate logic of love; In the isolated sex scene between the two (filmed months later, as it did not exist in the first version of the script), the only thing emphasized in the prudish dynamic of the shadows making out is the French kiss. But, continuing in this vein of scrutinizing the main points of the film, not even the rivalry with Iceman is well worked. The evident homoeroticism that exists in this relationship (see the malicious looks during the presentations, the scenes of horniness in the locker room and especially the blatant volleyball game between the shirtless men) does not serve to mobilize anything. In the end, "Top Gun" leaves no important message or reflection, it doesn't have a creative script and it doesn't even recycle old clichés. Tony Scott prefers to follow the opposite path, abusing formulas and recipes to achieve box office success. Therefore, he explores action scenes involving fighter jets to attract the male audience and romance involving the heartthrob of the time to attract the female audience. In the end, the director managed to achieve his goal, but unfortunately, he didn't achieve anything more than that. Unlike the powerful planes we see throughout the film, "Top Gun" never takes greater flights.

6.title: Fun, but not as fun as it could have been
6.content:
My Age: 13

Lt. Pete Mitchell "Maverick", played by Tom Cruise, and Goose, played by Anthony Edwards are chosen to go to Top Gun, a navy school where they teach the top 1% of aircraft aviators special skills. Maverick wants to be top of his class, but he has some competition, most notably "Iceman", played by Val Kilmer. He is also falling in love with his instructor, played by Kelly McGillis.

This film is nice and stylish, with some good aircraft training sequences, some good acting performances from Tom Cruise and most supporting roles, a lot of energy, and some fairly average romance. It is fun throughout most of its length, and the ending is pretty good. But it's a pity there is only one real flying scene. The rest is all just training, therefore no explosions and not as much fun as there could have been.

This film will always go down as an 80s classic with its appeal to both the lads and the ladies. The lads go for the action, the women go for the love story.

No doubt about it, the film has some amazing dog fights as well as a sturdy plot to emphasis its reasoning.

The overall cast was chosen well, Tom Cruise suited the cocky hero heart throb, as always. Kelly McGillis was the perfect choice to play the intelligent love interest, Val Kilmer played his best role to date as the rival Ice Man and Tom Skerrit was well chosen to play the warm hearted mentor.

It is not usually my cup of tea, but the romance side of it was not as bad as I expected because it for once had a realistic approach.

What let the film down for me was the stupid musical numbers, such as "you've lost that loving feeling" and "goodness gracious great balls of fire". As not only did it make the actors look stupid, but they were also unrealistic, how many times do you see that in real life? The film is also backed up by an awesome soundtrack, which gave the film that atmosphere.

Overall, a film that everyone should watch at least once in their life time.

6.title: The highway to the dangerzone is a road filled with cliches, bro-love, adrenaline and cheese

Tom Cruise is at his most charming as this is the film which cemented his star status following the brilliantly fun Risky Business and the supporting cast try their best with a script filled with high-fives and laddy 80s banter mixed in with a light sprinkling of tradgey which elevates the movie in the third act. 6.title: Fun flying, but narratively disappointing

All things said, Top Gun is understandably a classic movie. Maverick is charming, some scenes are emotional, and the action is tense. However, Top Gun is narratively disappointing.

The plot tends to jump around without much care for where the story leads, and it never feels consistent. A movie does not need to be predictable, but it should at least have a solid narrative. More than anything, Top Gun feels like a montage of scenes from a well-structured movie. Had the narrative been better, I could have found myself more engaged in the story. Instead we are left with a fun movie that leaves little room for thought.

Rating: D+

6.title: I got the need, the need for a quick rewrite
6.content:
Gosh, I wish I liked this more than I do. I mean, it's technically accomplished, there are some nice performances, it looks good, but the story is just so wane, the stakes so completely absent for so much of the running time, and the romance so generically dull that it seriously limits my enjoyment of what the film does well. It's just one of those films where the technical side of things is so high that it really does just come down to a balance between that and everything else that is just kind of...boring.

Pete Mitchell, Maverick, (Tom Cruise) is a hotshot naval aviator flying F-14s with his radar intercept officer, Nick, Goose, getting sent to Top Gun, the naval school for elite aviators to teach them dogfighting. The one piece of screenwriting that I actually appreciate in this film is how the beginning, where we watch the best aviator on the aircraft carrier, Cougar (John Stockwell), get so spooked by an encounter with potential enemy MiGs that he just outright quits. This gets repeated later in the film with Maverick which is the one bit of screenwriting structure that feels like it has some real thought in it. Because, otherwise, this is just Pete up against Tom Kazansky, Iceman, (Val Kilmer) about who's the best pilot at Top Gun.

When I say that there are no real stakes here, I really mean it. There's little sense that what they're doing is actually dangerous to them personally because none of the pilots are self-reflective enough to realize that they're doing incredibly dangerous things that can end their lives for roughly the first hour and twenty minutes of the film. Aside from the opening with Cougar, it's just a bunch of hotheads arguing about who's the best of the best. If it weren't matched with some incredible aerial footage of these aircraft dodging around each other, expertly edited together, it'd be a slog of boring machismo without any stakes.

And then there's the romance. Pete meets the civilian contractor, Charlotte (Kelly McGillis), and the two have this will they won't they relationship that's just honestly never that interesting. It's rote, at best, all the while we know that they'll get together in the end, that Pete's recklessness will temper just enough so that Charlotte can love him...except we don't even need to get that far. They' fall in love by the halfway point. I suppose it's a small mercy that she isn't one of those, "I'm always worried about losing you every time you go up," movie wives, but they've replaced that trope with almost nothing instead. It's just a dull as dishwater romance that eats up minutes and minutes of screentime.

Things get amplified during one of the training exercises when something terrible happens to a character, shaking Maverick's confidence to the point that he thinks of quitting the whole thing. Finally, there are stakes. This honestly would have worked better if the sense of danger were more palpable through the whole preceding couple of acts instead of just relying heavily on how awesome it is to fly fighter jets (which, admittedly, seems pretty awesome). And then it really becomes, can Maverick get over the fact that he's not really responsible for a tragedy and fly again? It's kind of an odd moment.

And the final act is actually, finally, a clearly defined dramatic situation where tensions are running high with some unnamed foreign power in the Indian Ocean, and there's going to be potential for violence during a rescue mission. Combine that with Maverick still trying to get over his mental blocks, and you've got the makings of a quality third act. It almost feels like an accident that it gets to that, to a third act that actually does kind of work, but there it is.

Also, the whole final moment with Iceman feels so unearned because the rivalry between the two was never that deep, just simplistic rivalry type stuff.

So...I'm mixed on the whole thing. The technical side of things is top notch. The third act works quite well while combining nicely with the prologue. However, everything in between is thin and dull, especially the romance. It's a rewrite away from giving the majority of the film stakes, diminishing the romance appropriately, and tying up the whole film with a stronger emotional throughline. Maybe a decades-later legacy sequel could do...all of those things?

6.title: It's an eh for me
6.content:
Let's get this clear: the flight sequences are amazing to watch. My whole family was ooh-ing and ah-ing during every single one, and we genuinely sensed the danger (and excitement) the fighter pilots were in. Soundtrack, loved it. Muscular, toned guys, check.

Story-wise though, there were a few moments-not going to spoil anything-that are supposedly important to Pete Mitchell, but it's not worked in sensitively and deeply such that the audience can also empathize with. In fact, this movie perplexed my parents (aged 49-54 years old) at times; if they didn't catch a single line about something, they wouldn't understand a character's motivation.

Okay, you might say, chill out it ain't that deep. But there was also a scene that lacked explanation (one character's only piece of dialogue near the end of movie). In addition to that, the movie felt kind of predictable. The main plot developments in the movie were nothing exciting and new. Honestly, it felt like checking off boxes.

I watched this movie, because the rest of my family had only seen Tom Cruise in Mission Impossible movies (known to us as mostly action, less varied acting), but I did enjoy Risky Business, so I had hoped to see another dimension of Tom Cruise here.

This quote from critic Roger Egert sums it up best: "Movies like Top Gun are hard to review because the good parts are so good and the bad parts are so relentless. The dogfights are absolutely the best since Clint Eastwood's electrifying aerial scenes in Firefox. But look out for the scenes where the people talk to one another."

6.title: Cool To See Young Tom Cruise
6.content:
I have been meaning to watch Top Gun Maverick due to its good reviews and high ratings, so I gave the first movie a go even if it is not a direct sequel as most people say.

Thankfully, I did not check its ratings online which I normally do, because I usually skip watching movies with low ratings. So I went to see it with zero expectations.

First of all, I think it's cool to see young Tom Cruise. He's a true action star and an entertainer and his on-screen charisma is undeniable. In terms of his emotional range as an actor, that I have yet to figure out since I don't watch a lot of his movies. But judging on this film, I would say it's just okay.

The plot is entertaining. Although it's kinda formulaic and a no-brainer type of film, in my opinion. But watching this in 2023, I would say the film's 80s aesthetic and soundtrack makes it more interesting than the plot. I don't think Tony Scott is trying to win an Oscar for this film.

I like the idea of fighter jets and dog fights, although in the film it could have given us more depth since it is what the film is about.

One of the best things about the film is Goose and Maverick's relationship. The connection felt real and effective. The death of Goose hit me in the feels. Goes to show how great Scott cemented their friendship in the story.

Overall, it's an average action film that's entertaining. Watching from a modern lens, I think some of the acting is a bit cheesy and dated.

6.title: If Nothing Else, Watch the Beautiful Aerial Photography!

6.title: Not great, good though.

6.title: Big Budget Cheese
6.content:
Top Gun has stood the test of time about as well as the Kenny Loggins songs featured in it. Which is to say, about 50/50.

Top Gun, despite receiving mediocre reviews from critics when it was released, was a blockbuster for Paramount Pictures, and the highest grossing movie of 1986.

The good: The visual effects still stand up nearly 40 years after its release. The biggest star of the movie is arguably the F14A Tomcat and best scenes are in the cockpit. Val Kilmer shines as Iceman, and Anthony Edwards and Meg Ryan put in solid performances.

The bad: nearly everything else. Stilted script and frequently wooden acting. Tom Cruise's character is a hopelessly arrogant pilot, who, in reality, would have been stripped of his wings for dangerous flying, not sent to Top Gun. The chemistry between Tom Cruise and Kelly McGillis is nonexistent, the entire soundtrack is 80s cheese. There are so many technical gaffes that is seems as though director Tony Scott didn't even bother to bring in technical support from a former fighter pilot. Some glaring examples: Throttles work in reverse (pilots pull the throttles to idle when supposedly throttling up) and dogfights that take place just off surface of the desert, when there is supposed to be a 10,000 ft hard floor that was important enough to be a plot point.

It's good, but not great. Director Tony Scott was much better than this. For a better Tony Scott experience, revisit "Enemy of the State" or "True Romance".
